title: Modelling krill growth, reproduction, and metabolism to predict life-history responses to environmental change
content:
Abstract
Allocation of energy is as important as energy uptake for maintaining healthy life cycles and sustainable populations of krill. Environmental factors such as temperature and food availability play important roles in the physiological performance of krill. This study adapted an established “Energetics Moult-Cycle (EMC) model” framework to investigate krill energy allocation and physiological responses under current and projected environment scenarios (low emission SSP2-4.5 and business-as-usual SSP5-8.5) by the end of this century from CMIP6 models, coupled with potential changes in food availability. Our results showed the model effectively regulated energy distribution among physiological functions, with distinct pathways channeling energy from lipid and protein sources. The results for growth trajectories, egg production, and lipid and protein body content aligned reasonably well with field observations. Food quality tests showed a strong link between lipid content of prey and krill reproductive success, with optimal reproductive performance when the diet consisted of 40% lipid and 60% protein. Under future conditions, our model indicates lower fecundity at older ages (3+ years) under the business-as-usual emission scenario. The case study based on information from South Georgia suggested that high water temperatures and insufficient carbon availability in the future pose a survival challenge for krill.
